items.title: L11: Reading a presentation brief and structuring it
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Promotion interviews at EO and HEO often include a presentation. The brief usually sets four things: the topic or question, the time limit, the audience and whether slides are allowed. Treat each as an instruction. The topic is a question to answer, not a subject to talk around. The time limit is firm, and panels commonly stop you when it expires. The audience matters because a presentation for senior managers who are not specialists needs plain language, explained acronyms and an early statement of what you want them to decide or understand.

A reliable structure has three parts. First, an opening that states the question in your own words and signposts what you will cover, for example two or three key messages. Second, the body, in which each message gets a short explanation backed by one piece of evidence or an example. Third, a close that repeats the main message and, where the brief asks for it, gives a clear recommendation with the main risk and how you would manage it.

Two or three messages is usually the most a listener can retain. Spend your preparation time deciding what to leave out. Do not spend long on background the audience already knows, because every minute of context is a minute taken from the answer. Slides, if allowed, should support you rather than replace you: a few simple slides with short phrases, never paragraphs you read aloud. Question time often follows and is scored too, so prepare for the obvious challenges, such as cost, risk and what you would do differently. If you need an adjustment, such as extra preparation time, ask through the recruitment contact before the day rather than on it.

questions.prompt: You are given a presentation topic and ten minutes of preparation time. Which first step is the most useful?

options.text: Pick your strongest prepared material and shape the topic around it, because depth of knowledge is what panels reward most
Write a full script so you can read it out word for word on the day
Pin down the exact question, the audience and the time limit from the brief
Draft the slides first so that the layout decides your key message

questions.hint: The brief defines what a good answer must do, so it comes before any content decisions.

questions.prompt: A brief allows ten minutes for the presentation, then questions. Which content plan is best?

options.text: Two or three key messages, each backed by one piece of evidence, with a little time to spare
One single point explored in depth until the ten minutes are fully used
As many points as will fit, leaving the supporting detail for question time
Six or seven points delivered briskly, so that every angle of the topic gets at least a mention before the time runs out

questions.hint: A small number of well-evidenced messages is easier for a panel to follow and score.

questions.prompt: The audience is described as senior managers who are not specialists in your policy area. What is the best adjustment?

options.text: Include the full technical detail, so that nobody on the panel can say you left out something that mattered to the subject
Keep the language specialist so that the panel can see how well you know the area
Stay neutral and avoid a view, as non-specialists prefer a balanced summary
Use plain language, explain acronyms and say early what you want them to take away

questions.hint: Presentations are judged on how well they communicate to the audience named in the brief.

questions.prompt: Why does a strong presentation open by signposting its two or three messages?

options.text: The panel is less likely to interrupt with questions before the end
The audience can follow the structure and sees a clear line of argument from the start
Nerves settle while you cover the outline, which gives you a calm minute before the real content of the talk begins
You can then shorten the conclusion, as the main point has already been made

questions.hint: Signposting helps listeners follow and shows structured thinking, scored under Communicating and Influencing.

questions.prompt: A candidate spends three minutes of a ten-minute presentation on the history of the policy. What is the main weakness?

options.text: Time that should answer the question goes on background the audience mostly knows
History is not evidence, so it should never appear in a presentation of this kind whatever the audience already knows
The candidate should have opened with the conclusion and left history out entirely
Three minutes is too brief to do justice to the history of a policy area

questions.hint: Context should be brief so that most of the time goes on the question that was set.

questions.prompt: With one minute left you still have one key point and the conclusion to give. What is the best move?

options.text: Speed up and cover both points in full, accepting that you will overrun by a minute or so, since completeness matters most
Give the point in a sentence or two, then close on your main message and recommendation
Pause and ask the panel whether they would like you to carry on past the limit
Drop the conclusion and use the last minute to finish the point properly

questions.hint: A controlled finish keeps to the limit and still delivers the conclusion.

questions.prompt: How should slides be used in an interview presentation?

options.text: Detailed slides the panel can study in their own time while you talk
None at all, since panels generally mark down any use of slides
A few simple slides with short phrases that support what you say aloud
One slide for each minute, each carrying the full text of what you will say

questions.hint: Slides support the speaker; reading dense text aloud loses the audience.

questions.prompt: The brief asks you to recommend one of three options. What must the presentation contain?

options.text: A clear recommendation, the reasons for it, and the main risk with how you would manage it
A fair description of all three options in turn, so that the panel can weigh them up and choose between them themselves
A recommendation on its own, with the reasoning saved for question time
A ranked list of the options that does not dwell on any drawbacks

questions.hint: A recommendation without reasoning and risk shows weaker judgement than the question asks for.

questions.prompt: Your laptop will not open the slides when you are about to start. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Tell the panel briefly and deliver from your notes, keeping to your structure
Read the presentation off your phone screen instead of using the slides
Keep trying to repair it for several minutes while the panel waits patiently
Ask the panel to reschedule the presentation so that you can give it in the form you planned, with your slides to hand

questions.hint: Composure and adaptability are assessed, and the content matters more than the slides.

questions.prompt: You need extra preparation time because of a condition that affects reading speed. When should you raise it?

options.text: Before the interview, through the recruitment contact named in the invitation
Only if the panel seems to notice that you are struggling
When you receive the brief, by telling the panel chair at the start
After the presentation, if you feel that the time limit held you back

questions.hint: Adjustments are arranged in advance so that they can actually be put in place.

items.title: L11: Written exercises under timed conditions
items.source: Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance and Success Profiles (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Some EO and HEO promotion processes include a written exercise, such as a briefing note, a short email to a senior colleague or a summary of a set of papers. It tests the Ability and Behaviours elements of Success Profiles, in particular Communicating and Influencing, and often Making Effective Decisions. You are normally given a fixed time, a scenario and a pack of information, some of it irrelevant.

A useful sequence is read, plan, write, check. Spend the first part of the time reading the task and underlining what the reader needs: who they are, what decision or action is required and by when. Then plan in a few lines: the main message, the two or three supporting points, and any recommendation. Writing without a plan is the most common cause of a rambling answer that runs out of time before reaching a conclusion.

Civil Service writing puts the conclusion first. A briefing note usually opens with a short summary or recommendation, followed by the key facts, the options or risks, and the next steps. Use short sentences, plain words and clear headings, and write for a reader who is busy and may not know the detail. Do not copy large parts of the pack. The assessors want to see you select what matters and leave out the rest.

Give the last few minutes to checking: the recommendation answers the question that was set, figures match the source papers, names and dates are right, and there are no spelling or grammar slips. If you notice a conflict or error in the pack, flag it to the reader rather than silently choosing one version. If time runs out, finish with your recommendation, even if it is brief.

questions.prompt: In a timed written exercise, what most often causes avoidable loss of marks?

options.text: Keeping sentences short, which can look under-developed to a marker
Writing straight away without a plan, so the answer rambles and no conclusion is reached
Reading the information pack too closely before you begin to write, because that uses up time you needed for drafting
Using headings, as they take time away from the substance of the answer

questions.hint: A short plan keeps the answer focused and ensures the conclusion arrives before time runs out.

questions.prompt: A briefing note is going to a busy director. Where should the recommendation normally appear?

options.text: In the middle, between the background and the options
At the end of the note, after the director has read the full argument and seen how the evidence builds up to a conclusion
In a covering email, with the note itself kept neutral
Right at the start, in a short summary, with the supporting detail after it

questions.hint: Civil Service writing leads with the conclusion so that a busy reader gets the point at once.

questions.prompt: The information pack includes a long appendix that is only partly relevant. How should you treat it?

options.text: Summarise every section in turn so that nothing from the pack is missing and the assessors can see you read all of it
Refer to the appendix and tell the reader to look through it themselves
Pick out the points the reader needs and leave the rest unmentioned
Copy across the main tables to show the assessors you found them

questions.hint: Selection and prioritisation are what the exercise tests, not completeness.

questions.prompt: While writing, you notice two papers give different figures for the same cost. What is the best action?

options.text: Use the better-evidenced figure and tell the reader about the inconsistency
Average the two figures so that you are not seen to take sides
Use the higher figure to be cautious and say nothing about the other, because an overestimate is safer than an underestimate
Leave the cost out so that the note cannot contain a wrong figure

questions.hint: Flagging a discrepancy shows integrity and sound judgement and lets the reader decide.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a final check of a written exercise?

options.text: The recommendation answers the question set, figures match the source and there are no slips
A spelling check only, as the content cannot sensibly change by then
Extra background added so that the answer looks more thorough
A rewrite of the opening paragraph so that it reads in a more impressive and polished style before you hand the note in

questions.hint: A final check catches errors of substance as well as presentation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence suits a briefing note for a senior reader?

options.text: We recommend extending the pilot by three months, because early results show lower costs.
It might perhaps be worth considering whether the pilot could possibly be extended.
Extension of the pilot is a matter on which views differ and analysis is still awaited.
The pilot, set up some time ago, has a number of aspects that may be of interest.

questions.hint: Plain, direct sentences that state the recommendation and its reason suit a busy reader.

questions.prompt: Five minutes remain and your note is half-finished. What should you do?

options.text: Write the recommendation and next steps briefly, even if the supporting detail is thin
Start again with a shorter version that you can finish in the time left
Complete the section you are on in full and let the reader infer the rest, since a finished section scores better than a rushed list
Add a line telling the assessors the exercise is unfinished and stop

questions.hint: A clear recommendation is the part the reader needs most and assessors usually reward.

questions.prompt: The task is to write to a colleague who has little time and no background. Which opening is strongest?

options.text: A list of every document you reviewed in preparing the note
One or two sentences stating the problem, your recommendation and the action needed
A question asking whether they would like more detail before you continue
A paragraph thanking the colleague for their time and tracing the history of the project before you reach the request

questions.hint: The reader should know what is needed from them within the first lines.

questions.prompt: Why do written exercises often include irrelevant or poorly organised papers?

options.text: To see whether you notice formatting errors in the source papers
To check that you can summarise every document in the pack fairly and without bias, whether or not it is relevant to the task
To make the time limit feel realistic without it affecting the marking
To test whether you can separate essential information from the rest and prioritise

questions.hint: Prioritising under time pressure is a core skill in policy and operational roles.

questions.prompt: Which element of Success Profiles do written exercises most obviously test alongside Behaviours?

options.text: Experience, through the length of your career
Strengths, through what you enjoy writing about
Technical, through knowledge of the department's policy
Ability, for example reasoning and written communication

questions.hint: Ability covers skills such as reasoning and communication, which a written task shows directly.

items.title: L11: Panel roles and how scoring works
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles and Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body:
Interview panels for EO and HEO roles usually have two or three members, sometimes more. One acts as chair, who welcomes you, explains the process, keeps to time and makes sure each question is asked fairly. Panellists put the questions, write notes and score. In many panels, someone from outside the hiring team is included to protect fairness. Panels are trained and are expected to follow the Civil Service Recruitment Principles, which require appointment on merit after fair and open competition.

Each panellist normally scores each answer independently against the criteria for the role, using a marking scheme with descriptors for each score. The scores are then compared and, where they differ, the panel discusses the evidence and agrees a final mark. This moderation is why your answer needs to give clear, specific evidence: the panel can only score what you actually say, not what they assume about you.

Panellists are not trying to catch you out. They often avoid giving feedback during the interview, so a neutral face or a lack of nodding does not tell you how you are doing. Note-taking is routine and does not mean you have said something wrong. A panellist who knows you, or a candidate, should declare it. A panel should not score you on anything that is not in the criteria, such as your accent, your age or whether you are similar to them.

In practice: address your answer mainly to the person who asked, but include the others with eye contact; check you have answered the whole question; and ask for a question to be repeated if needed. Treat every panellist with the same courtesy, as all contribute to the final decision.

questions.prompt: What is the chair of an interview panel mainly responsible for?

options.text: Taking the final decision alone, whatever the other panellists have scored, because someone must be accountable for the result
Giving candidates informal feedback as the interview goes along
Deciding the questions on the day depending on how each candidate does
Explaining the process, keeping to time and ensuring each candidate is treated fairly

questions.hint: The chair manages the process, while the decision rests on every panellist's evidence-based score.

questions.prompt: Why is a panellist's neutral expression not a reliable sign of how you are doing?

options.text: Panels hide disappointment but always show approval, so a blank face usually means a middling answer rather than a poor one
Panels are trained to stay neutral during the interview and to score afterwards
A neutral face shows the panel has already made its decision about you
Panellists are told not to look at candidates while they are answering

questions.hint: Panels avoid signalling views so that every candidate is treated consistently.

questions.prompt: Two panellists score the same answer differently. What usually happens next?

options.text: The question is asked again so the answer can be rescored
The higher of the two scores stands, because the candidate should receive the benefit of any doubt in the panel's view
They compare the evidence and agree a final mark
The chair's score replaces the other scores

questions.hint: Moderation uses the evidence given in the answer to reach an agreed mark.

questions.prompt: What does moderation mean for how you structure answers?

options.text: Keep answers general so that every panellist can read them favourably and none of them has a reason to score you down
Keep answers shorter so that there is less room for disagreement
Repeat your best example so that all the panel remember it
Give specific, observable evidence so panellists can justify their scores

questions.hint: Panels can only score the evidence you actually give them.

questions.prompt: You recognise one panellist as someone you worked with years ago. What should you do?

options.text: Say nothing so that you do not cause awkwardness at the start, as raising it could make the panel treat you differently
Ask for a different panellist if you think they may not rate you
Mention it politely to the chair so that it can be handled openly
Greet them warmly and refer to the shared history in your answers

questions.hint: Prior relationships should be declared so that the panel can manage fairness concerns.

questions.prompt: During your answer a panellist keeps writing notes without looking up. How should you read this?

options.text: As a cue to repeat your last point more slowly
As a sign that your answer is not going well and that you should change direction, speed up or add some further detail
As normal practice, since they are recording evidence to score later
As an invitation to pause until they have finished writing

questions.hint: Note-taking is how panels record evidence and says little about quality.

questions.prompt: On which basis may a panel legitimately score you?

options.text: Whether you seem like someone they would enjoy working with
Your accent and how confident you sound compared with others
How similar your background and interests are to the panel's own, since fit with the team is part of any appointment
The evidence you give against the criteria for the role

questions.hint: Scoring must stick to the published criteria; similarity to the panel is a form of bias.

questions.prompt: A question is long and you remember only the first half. What is the best course?

options.text: Wait quietly until they decide to repeat it
Answer the half you remember and hope that it is enough, because asking for a repeat can look as though you were not listening
Ask the panellist politely to repeat the question
Give a broad answer on the general topic that might cover both parts

questions.hint: Asking for clarification avoids answering the wrong question and is acceptable.

questions.prompt: Which Recruitment Principle explains why panels use structured questions and marking schemes?

options.text: Appointment at the discretion of the most senior panellist
Appointment according to length of service
Appointment through internal networks before outside candidates
Appointment on merit after fair and open competition

questions.hint: Structured assessment against published criteria is how merit is applied consistently.

questions.prompt: In a three-person panel, to whom should you direct your answer?

options.text: Only to the chair, as the person who finalises the decision, because looking round the panel can seem unfocused
Only to the panellist who is writing the notes
Mainly to the person who asked, with eye contact shared across the panel
Only to the most senior person present, who has the greatest say

questions.hint: All panellists score, so include everyone while answering the person who asked.

items.title: L11: Strengths-based interviews for promotion
items.body:
Strengths-based questions look at what you do well and enjoy, rather than at a specific past example. In the Civil Service, strengths are defined as things that we do regularly, do well and that motivate us. A strengths interview usually has more questions than a Behaviours interview, each shorter, and moves quickly. A typical set includes questions such as what you enjoy doing most at work, what you find hardest, or what you would do first if given a new team. Questions may also include a short scenario.

Panels look for three signals: how you talk (energy and enthusiasm), what you do (evidence that you perform well) and why you care. Typical scoring pays attention to how quickly and naturally you respond, so over-rehearsed answers can sound flat. You cannot prepare specific answers in the way you can for Behaviours, but you can prepare by reflecting on your own strengths and thinking of everyday examples that show them. Read the advert and the strengths listed for the role, and consider which of your natural strengths match.

At EO and HEO, strengths questions may touch on people and delivery: what energises you about developing others, how you react when plans change, or what you do when work is behind. Answer honestly. Claiming a strength you do not have may create difficulty later, and panels often test authenticity with a follow-up. Answers need not use STAR, but giving a short example makes a strength credible. Be brief: strengths questions reward concise, natural responses. Saying that you enjoy something and showing an example where it helped a colleague or the team is stronger than a long account.

questions.prompt: How do the Civil Service Success Profiles define strengths?

options.text: Qualifications that match the job description closely
Behaviours that scored highly at previous interviews
Technical skills we have learned through formal training
Things we do regularly, do well and that motivate us

questions.hint: Strengths combine performance and energy, not just skill.

questions.prompt: Compared with a Behaviours interview, a strengths interview usually has

options.text: more questions, each answered more briefly
the same number of questions but no scoring
extra written preparation time before it starts
fewer questions, each answered at greater length so that the panel can see a full example from start to finish

questions.hint: Strengths interviews move at pace and capture more spontaneous responses.

questions.prompt: Which signals will a panel most likely look for when scoring a strengths answer?

options.text: A full STAR answer with all four parts for every question, because panels cannot score without a complete story
Energy and enthusiasm together with evidence of doing the thing well
Agreement with the panel's own views on what matters
The longest and most detailed answer given by any candidate

questions.hint: Strengths scoring weighs what you enjoy and what you do well.

questions.prompt: Asked 'What do you find hardest at work?', which answer is strongest?

options.text: A strength presented as a weakness, such as working too hard, because it shows you can turn a negative into a positive
An honest challenge, with a short example of how you manage it
A long account of a past failure that ends without a lesson
A statement that nothing at work is especially difficult

questions.hint: Honesty with awareness and a coping approach shows authenticity and growth.

questions.prompt: Why can heavily rehearsed answers hurt in a strengths interview?

options.text: Rehearsed answers tend to run well over the time allowed
They suggest that you have misread the Success Profiles
The interview rules do not allow candidates to prepare answers in advance, so anything rehearsed can be marked down
They can sound flat and lack the natural energy panels look for

questions.hint: Strengths are partly judged on how naturally and quickly you respond.

questions.prompt: How can you best prepare for strengths questions?

options.text: Reflect on what you enjoy and do well, think of everyday examples, and read the role's listed strengths
Memorise the department's annual report and priorities
Write one STAR example for each Behaviour in the role
Learn model answers from interview websites

questions.hint: You prepare by knowing yourself and your evidence rather than by scripting.

questions.prompt: A panel asks, 'What would you do first with a new team?' Which answer fits an HEO strengths question best?

options.text: Review the structure chart and set new targets within the first week
Meet each person to understand their work, then agree with them what to deliver first
Change the team's processes straight away to show direction
Rely on the previous manager's handover until you know the team

questions.hint: Listening before leading reflects the people-management focus of senior roles.

questions.prompt: You say you enjoy coaching colleagues. How might the panel test whether that is true?

options.text: With a follow-up asking for a recent example and what you did
With a written test on coaching theory after the interview, which checks that your claims rest on genuine knowledge
By asking you to name colleagues you have coached
By asking about your hobbies and interests outside work

questions.hint: Authenticity is checked through short, specific follow-up questions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about STAR in strengths interviews is correct?

options.text: It must be used in full for every question
It applies only to questions about technical skills
It is not allowed because it sounds too rehearsed
It is not required, but a brief example makes a strength more credible

questions.hint: Short evidence strengthens a claim without turning the answer into a long story.

questions.prompt: A candidate claims a strength they do not really have because it suits the job. What is the main risk?

options.text: The panel may probe it and the answer may unravel, and the role may not suit them
The candidate may be given a written test on the strength
The panel may credit the ambition behind the claim
None, as a panel has no means to verify strengths in the room and so cannot tell a genuine claim from a convenient one

questions.hint: Authentic strengths match the role better and withstand probing.

items.title: L11: Leadership behaviour at EO and HEO
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours framework (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Leadership is one of the Civil Service Behaviours, and it is assessed more heavily as you move into supervisory and management roles. At EO level and above, it is about being a role model, setting direction and getting the best from people, not about rank. You can show leadership without a formal title, for example by leading a small project, by guiding a new starter or by taking responsibility for improving a process.

Typical effective behaviours at this level include being honest and fair in how you treat people, communicating clearly why work matters, giving people clarity about what is expected, and recognising achievement. Leaders also deal with problems early: they have the difficult conversation about poor performance rather than hoping it will resolve, and they stay calm and constructive when plans change. Ineffective behaviours include avoiding decisions, blaming others, taking credit for the team's work and being inconsistent in how people are treated.

In an interview, panels want evidence of what you personally did to lead. A strong example identifies the situation in which others needed direction, the specific actions you took, such as setting objectives, allocating work to suit people's strengths or giving feedback, and the result, including how the team performed or developed. For a HEO, panels expect examples in which you led others through change or delivered through a team, rather than only your own tasks.

Be ready to talk about mistakes. A good leadership answer includes what you learned from something that did not go to plan, and how you changed your approach. Avoid describing leadership purely as being in charge or instructing others.

questions.prompt: At EO level, what does the Leadership behaviour mainly assess?

options.text: How long you have served in the Civil Service
Whether you hold a recognised leadership qualification
How many people you manage on paper in the structure chart, since line-management span is the usual measure of leadership
Whether you act as a role model, set direction and bring out the best in others

questions.hint: Leadership is shown through behaviour, not title or number of reports.

questions.prompt: Which example best evidences leadership for an EO with no direct reports?

options.text: Being asked by your manager to cover during a short absence
Finishing a leadership course and passing the assessment at the end
Taking charge of a small project, agreeing roles and keeping the group on track
Completing your own tasks well and ahead of time every month, so that colleagues look to you as an example of good practice

questions.hint: Leading others, even informally, is the evidence panels look for.

questions.prompt: A team member's performance is slipping. Which approach reflects effective leadership?

options.text: Hold an early, constructive conversation to understand causes and agree support and expectations
Give their harder tasks to others so that deadlines are still met
Wait for a few weeks to see whether it improves before saying anything, so that you act on a proper pattern rather than a bad patch
Raise it in a team meeting so that standards improve for everyone

questions.hint: Effective leaders deal with performance concerns early, fairly and privately.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an ineffective leadership behaviour?

options.text: Taking credit for the team's achievements in front of senior managers
Explaining to the team why a piece of work matters and how it connects to what the department is trying to achieve
Setting out clear expectations when work is allocated
Recognising a colleague's contribution in public

questions.hint: Credit-taking undermines trust and is the opposite of leading by example.

questions.prompt: A candidate says, 'I led by telling people what to do and checking they did it.' What is missing?

options.text: Evidence that they gave out clear instructions, which shows direction, together with more detail about the deadline they worked to
A statement of their grade at the time
How they motivated and developed people and adapted to individuals
More detail about the deadline they worked to

questions.hint: Panels expect leadership to involve motivation and development, not only direction.

questions.prompt: Besides the situation and your actions, what should a strong leadership answer include?

options.text: A description of the managerial qualifications you hold
The result, including how the team performed or developed
A summary of the department's structure and purpose
A list of the team members' names and roles, so that the panel can follow who was involved in each part of the work

questions.hint: Results show the effect your actions had on others.

questions.prompt: For HEO roles, panels typically expect leadership examples that show

options.text: presenting to a senior audience on one occasion
leading others through change or delivering through a team
completing your own work to a consistently high standard
covering for your manager for a few days

questions.hint: Delivery through others marks the step up to HEO.

questions.prompt: Why include a mistake in a leadership answer?

options.text: It gives you a way to shorten the rest of the answer
It shows self-awareness and how you changed your approach afterwards
It proves that you are willing to take on risky work, which panels tend to value in people moving into management
It lets you avoid describing the result of your actions

questions.hint: Learning from setbacks is part of credible leadership.

questions.prompt: Priorities change suddenly midway through a project. Which response shows the most effective leadership?

options.text: Reassign tasks without explanation to save time
Tell the team to carry on as before until formal confirmation arrives
Explain what has changed and why, agree what to stop, and check people understand their new priorities
Wait for guidance from above before saying anything to the team, so that you do not pass on a message that later changes

questions.hint: Clear and timely communication helps teams adapt to change.

questions.prompt: Which statement about leadership in the Civil Service is correct?

options.text: It is demonstrated by working longer hours than the team
It can be shown at any grade through what you do
It begins only once you have line-management responsibility, because before that you cannot direct anyone else's work
It is mainly about making decisions on your own

questions.hint: The Civil Service treats leadership as behaviour available at every level.

items.title: L11: Describing people-management examples
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours; ACAS guidance on managing performance and absence
items.body:
For HEO and some EO roles, panels ask for examples of managing people: handling performance, supporting wellbeing, managing absence, giving feedback, or building a team. These situations involve personal information and legal duties, so how you describe them also tests judgement and the Civil Service Code.

Confidentiality matters. Describe the situation without naming or identifying individuals, and do not reveal sensitive details such as health conditions. Panels would be concerned by a candidate who discussed a colleague's health in a way that could identify them. Say 'a team member who was struggling with workload' rather than their name or diagnosis.

Management of performance usually follows a fair, staged pattern: spotting the problem early; having a private, factual conversation; agreeing clear expectations, support and a time to review; following the department's policy and involving HR where required; keeping records; and reviewing progress. In an interview, show that you used the process fairly rather than going straight to the formal stage, and that you also considered whether the cause was workload, skills or personal circumstances. Where wellbeing or absence is involved, mention supportive steps such as a return-to-work conversation and appropriate adjustments.

When talking about a team you built or developed, say what you personally did: how you assigned work to strengths, gave feedback, and arranged development, with outcomes such as improved quality or a colleague gaining confidence. Avoid presenting colleagues as obstacles. Panels often probe, asking what you would do differently, so be honest about limits and what the manager or HR contributed.

questions.prompt: You describe a performance case in an interview. How should you refer to the colleague involved?

options.text: By first name, since the panel keeps interview content confidential
By initials and the name of their team
Without identifying them, for example as 'a team member'
By name and job title so that the example is clear

questions.hint: Confidentiality applies to interview examples, and panels notice whether you protect it.

questions.prompt: A candidate gives the exact health condition of a colleague while describing an absence case. What is the problem?

options.text: It makes the example more credible and detailed, which helps the panel to judge how serious the case was
It is a problem only if the colleague is named
It breaks no rule, because the panel is also in the Civil Service
It discloses sensitive personal information and shows poor judgement

questions.hint: Health information is sensitive and must not be shared in a way that could identify someone.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best reflects a fair approach to a performance concern?

options.text: Monitor quietly for months, then act on the accumulated record
Mention it in the team meeting, then act if nothing changes
Early private conversation, agreed expectations and support, then review while following policy
Formal warning first, with support offered only if there is no improvement, so that the expectations are on record from day one

questions.hint: Fair processes start early and supportively, with proper records.

questions.prompt: Before treating a drop in performance as a capability problem, what should a manager consider?

options.text: How long the person has been in the team
Whether other teams have had the same experience
Whether workload, skills, health or personal circumstances are contributing
Whether the person is well liked in the team, since a strained working relationship can affect how the work is judged

questions.hint: Understanding causes is part of a fair and effective approach.

questions.prompt: After a colleague returns from sickness absence, which step is usually good practice?

options.text: Extra work to help them catch up quickly, so that the backlog from their absence does not fall on colleagues
Telling the team why the colleague was away
A return-to-work conversation, with adjustments where appropriate
Avoiding the subject so that they do not feel uncomfortable

questions.hint: Supportive conversations help wellbeing and allow reasonable adjustments.

questions.prompt: A panel asks about developing a team member. Which detail best shows what you personally did?

options.text: Development opportunities were available through the department
They improved a great deal over the year
I matched their tasks to their strengths, gave weekly feedback and arranged a short secondment
The team gave them a lot of opportunities to grow and take on new work over the course of the year

questions.hint: The answer should show your own actions rather than general circumstances.

questions.prompt: The panel asks what you would do differently in a case you managed. How should you respond?

options.text: Name a real improvement, for example acting earlier or involving HR sooner
Point to the process or the individual as the source of the difficulty
Say you would change nothing because the outcome was good, as the process clearly worked and the person improved
Say that you cannot recall enough to judge

questions.hint: Honest reflection shows learning and credibility.

questions.prompt: Why mention the role HR or your own manager played in a people-management example?

options.text: It shows you know when to seek advice and follow policy
It makes the answer longer and so more thorough
It lets you reduce the weight of your own contribution, so that the panel sees the case as a shared decision
It shows that you prefer others to take responsibility

questions.hint: Appropriate escalation shows judgement, provided your own actions are still clear.

questions.prompt: Which description of a colleague is most appropriate in an interview answer?

options.text: A colleague who was lazy about learning the system
One of my staff who kept letting the team down
A team member who found the new system difficult
A problem person in my team

questions.hint: Describing people neutrally and without blame reflects fairness and respect.

questions.prompt: Which outcome is the strongest evidence in a team-development example?

options.text: The team held a meeting about development
The colleague attended three training sessions during the year, as arranged under the development plan agreed with them
The colleague thanked you at the end of the process
The colleague's quality of work improved and they took on more responsibility

questions.hint: Outcomes should show an actual change in capability or performance.

items.title: L11: Probing questions and holding your account together
items.body:
After your first answer, panels often follow up with probing questions. They are a normal part of Behaviours interviews and are not a sign that you answered badly. The purpose is to get evidence that the first answer did not give: panels need enough detail to score, and they check that the example is real and that your role was what you said it was.

Common probes include: 'What exactly did you do?', 'Why did you decide that?', 'What was the result?', 'How did you know it had worked?', 'What did others think?' and 'What would you do differently?' A weak response is to repeat the answer or to add more background. A stronger approach is to answer the probe directly, with concrete detail: a decision, a reason, a number, a quote from feedback.

Your best protection is a clear account. For each example, know the sequence of events, who was involved, your specific actions, the measurable or observable result and what you learned. If you do not know a detail, such as an exact figure, say so honestly and give the best estimate with the source, rather than inventing one. Inconsistencies are noticed: if your first answer said you led the work and the probe reveals that a colleague made the key decisions, the panel will reduce its confidence in the whole answer.

If a probe is difficult, pause briefly, then answer. If you did not do something, say so and describe what you did instead. A probe on a mistake is a chance to show learning. Keep the same example throughout; changing to a new story partway through suggests the original was thin.

questions.prompt: After your answer, the panel asks 'What exactly did you do?' What does this most likely mean?

options.text: They need more specific evidence of your own actions to score the answer
They would like you to move on to the next question
Your answer was wrong and has to be replaced with another example, which the panel will then ask you to describe
They do not believe that the example is true

questions.hint: Probes seek missing evidence and are normal in Behaviours interviews.

questions.prompt: Which reply best answers the probe 'How did you know it had worked?'

options.text: It seemed to be better afterwards, and several colleagues told me that the new process had made their work easier
Everyone involved was happy with the result
The error rate fell from one in ten cases to one in twenty, and an audit confirmed it
It worked because we followed the agreed process

questions.hint: A specific, checkable measure shows impact better than an impression.

questions.prompt: You cannot recall the exact figure a panellist asks about. What is the best response?

options.text: Say you are unsure of the exact figure and give your best estimate and where it came from
Say that the exact figure was not important to the outcome
Move on quickly to your next point and hope they do not return to it
Give a precise figure that sounds right so that the answer stays credible and the panel does not lose confidence

questions.hint: Honesty is part of the Civil Service Code, and a caveated estimate is acceptable.

questions.prompt: Asked 'What would you do differently?', which answer shows the strongest learning?

options.text: I would have consulted the finance team earlier, as late changes cost us a week
I would have wanted more time to carry it out
I would have asked for a stronger team to deliver it
Nothing, as the project met its targets

questions.hint: Specific lessons show reflection and a willingness to improve.

questions.prompt: Your first answer said you led the work, but a probe shows a colleague made the key decisions. What is the effect?

options.text: The panel will treat it as strong teamwork and score higher
The panel loses confidence in the account and may lower the score
None, because the first answer has already been scored and the panel does not revisit marks after a probe
It makes the answer more modest and therefore stronger

questions.hint: Inconsistency between claim and detail damages credibility.

questions.prompt: A probe is difficult. What is a sensible approach?

options.text: Answer at once with whatever comes to mind first, as hesitating can look like uncertainty about your own example
Pause briefly to think, then answer it directly
Repeat your earlier answer in different words
Ask to move to the next question

questions.hint: A short pause is acceptable and leads to a more accurate answer.

questions.prompt: Midway through probing you realise the example is thin. What is the best course?

options.text: Switch to a different example that you think is stronger, as the panel will give credit for the better material
Tell the panel the example was not good enough
Fill the gaps with details you did not actually experience
Stay with it, give the real detail you have and be honest about the limits

questions.hint: Switching or embellishing damages credibility more than a limited but honest account.

questions.prompt: Which probe is most directly aimed at testing your decision-making?

options.text: Why did you choose that option rather than the alternatives?
When exactly did this happen?
Who else was in the team at the time and how much responsibility each of them had for the work?
What was your job title in that role?

questions.hint: Asking for the reasoning behind a choice assesses judgement.

questions.prompt: For each example, what should you have clear in your mind so that probing goes well?

options.text: A list of the people who could confirm it
The sequence, who was involved, your specific actions, the result and the learning
Only the successful ending
A script of the exact words to use

questions.hint: Knowing the details of your own story allows flexible, consistent answers.

questions.prompt: Asked 'What did others think?', you did not seek others' views at the time. What is the best response?

options.text: Say so honestly, then describe what feedback you received later and how you would gather views now
Say that everyone agreed, as nobody objected at the time and the work was delivered without complaint
Say that it did not matter what others thought
Name a senior person who approved the work

questions.hint: Truthful answers combined with learning keep credibility.

items.title: L11: Turning 'we' into 'I' without overclaiming
items.body:
Panels score what you did, not what your team did. A common weakness is describing everything as 'we': 'we launched the process, we reduced the backlog'. The panel then has no evidence of your own contribution, and the answer may score low even when the result was impressive. The opposite error is claiming credit for work that others did. Good answers sit between the two.

Use 'we' for the context and the shared result, and 'I' for your decisions and actions. For example: 'The team had a backlog of two hundred cases. I analysed the delays and found that most arose at one approval step. I proposed removing a duplicate check, I agreed it with the compliance lead and I trained the team in the new process. Together we cleared the backlog in six weeks.' The sentence about the team's overall result is fine, because the preceding sentences show your role.

When the panel asks 'What was your part?', answer in specific verbs: analysed, proposed, negotiated, decided, trained, escalated. Avoid vague verbs such as 'helped', 'was involved in' and 'supported', unless you then say how. Giving credit to others is a strength in leadership: saying 'a colleague spotted the problem, and I decided how to respond' is honest and shows you value people. It is acceptable and often good to say what others did, provided your own contribution is still clear.

Be honest. If the work was shared, say what proportion or element was yours. Panels may check references or talk to your manager, and exaggeration breaches the honesty required by the Civil Service Code.

questions.prompt: A candidate says, 'We reduced the backlog by half.' What is the main problem?

options.text: The panel cannot tell what the candidate personally did
The result is too small to impress a panel, as a halving of a backlog is a modest outcome at this grade
Backlogs are normally reduced by one person, not a team
The sentence is too short to be a full answer

questions.hint: Panels score individual contribution, which 'we' leaves unclear.

questions.prompt: Which version is the strongest account of a personal contribution?

options.text: I analysed where delays occurred, proposed removing a duplicate check and trained the team in the change
The process change succeeded thanks to the efforts of the team
I was involved in the process change that improved the backlog
We looked at where delays occurred and worked on the process together

questions.hint: Specific action verbs show exactly what you did.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is least helpful when describing your own role?

options.text: I decided the scope
I negotiated the timetable
I presented the findings
I helped with the project

questions.hint: 'Helped' hides what you did unless you explain how.

questions.prompt: A colleague spotted the original problem. How should you handle that in your answer?

options.text: Credit them, while making your own decision and actions clear
Credit them only if the panel asks about it
Credit them only if they are more senior than you
Leave them out so that the example focuses on you, because the panel is scoring your contribution and not theirs

questions.hint: Crediting others shows leadership and honesty without losing your own contribution.

questions.prompt: Where is 'we' most appropriate in a strong answer?

options.text: For the actions that did not go well
For every action in the story from beginning to end, as the work was done by the team and not by individuals
For none of the story, since every sentence should say 'I'
For the shared context and overall outcome, after you have explained your own actions

questions.hint: 'We' is fine when your own actions are already clear.

questions.prompt: A panellist asks: 'What was your part in that?' Which reply is best?

options.text: I mostly did what I was asked to do
I wrote the business case, secured sign-off from finance and then briefed the team
I supported it from the sidelines and kept an eye on progress
I was one of the team and we all pulled together

questions.hint: The probe asks for personal detail, so answer with specific actions.

questions.prompt: A candidate claims sole credit for a project that a colleague largely ran. What is the main risk?

options.text: It is acceptable if the result was good
It will earn extra marks for confidence
Overclaiming breaches honesty and may be exposed by probing or references
None, as candidates are expected to sell themselves and the panel knows that every example is told from one point of view

questions.hint: Honesty is a core Civil Service value, and claims can be checked.

questions.prompt: The work was shared equally between three people. How should you describe it?

options.text: Say it was shared and explain clearly which parts you owned
Choose another example where you worked alone
Say that you mainly observed, to avoid overclaiming
Describe the whole project as yours, since you were involved throughout and the panel can only score what you claim

questions.hint: Accurate attribution is honest and still shows your contribution.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives credit to others while keeping your role clear?

options.text: I did all of the work myself
A colleague spotted the issue and I decided how we should respond
The credit really belongs to the department
My team did everything and I just signed it off

questions.hint: It acknowledges others and shows your own decision-making.

questions.prompt: Why might a manager or referee be contacted after an interview?

options.text: To replace the panel's scoring with their own, which carries more weight because it is based on long working knowledge of you
To give you feedback on the interview
To decide which grade you will be offered
To confirm that the claims in your examples are accurate

questions.hint: References and checks can verify the evidence offered at interview.

items.title: L11: Case-study exercises
items.source: Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance and Success Profiles (GOV.UK)
items.body:
A case-study exercise gives you a realistic work scenario, often with a short pack of papers, and asks for analysis and a recommendation, either in writing or as a discussion with the panel. It tests Making Effective Decisions, Communicating and Influencing and sometimes Seeing the Big Picture. You are not expected to know the department's specific policy. You are expected to reason clearly with the information provided.

A sound approach has four stages. First, understand the situation: what is the problem, who is affected and what is the deadline? Second, identify the facts that matter and any gaps or inconsistencies in the information. Third, consider options, with the advantages, risks and costs of each, including the option of doing nothing. Fourth, recommend one option, explain why, and set out the next steps and how you would manage the main risk.

Watch for common mistakes. Candidates often jump to a solution before they have understood the problem; fail to compare options; rely on assumptions that are not in the papers without saying so; or forget the people affected, such as service users or colleagues. Panels reward a clear line of reasoning more than a particular answer, since many case studies have no single right answer.

If the exercise is a discussion, think aloud in a structured way and say what you would want to find out before deciding. If you must make assumptions, state them. Where the scenario touches on public money, fairness or confidentiality, show that you recognise the Civil Service Code and the relevant principles. Close with a short summary of your recommendation.

questions.prompt: What is a case-study exercise mainly designed to assess?

options.text: How you reason through a realistic situation to a justified recommendation
How quickly you can type up your thoughts
How much you already know about departmental policy and procedure, since you will be expected to apply it in the role
Whether you can memorise a pack of papers

questions.hint: The exercise looks at your reasoning with the information given, not specialist knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which is the best first stage in tackling a case study?

options.text: List every fact in the papers in the order they appear
Write the conclusion so you know where you are heading
Choose a solution and look for evidence to support it, which saves time in a short exercise and gives the answer a clear direction
Understand the problem, who is affected and the deadline

questions.hint: Understanding the problem prevents solutions that miss the point.

questions.prompt: The papers give two conflicting figures for one cost. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the panel which figure to use
Use the larger figure to be safe and carry on
Note the inconsistency, say which figure you rely on and why, and how you would check
Leave the cost out of the analysis

questions.hint: Identifying gaps and conflicts shows analytical care.

questions.prompt: What does a strong comparison of options include?

options.text: The cheapest option only, with its costs set out in full, because value for money is the main test in public service
A list of positives for the preferred option
The option the panel appears to favour
Advantages, risks and costs of each option, including doing nothing

questions.hint: Weighing alternatives openly shows balanced judgement.

questions.prompt: You need information that is not in the papers. What is the best approach?

options.text: Decline to make a recommendation without the data
Invent a reasonable figure to complete the analysis, because a full answer with an assumed number scores above an incomplete one
Carry on as if the gap were not there
State a reasonable assumption openly and say how you would test it

questions.hint: Stating assumptions keeps your reasoning transparent and honest.

questions.prompt: A candidate recommends an option without mentioning its drawbacks. What is missing?

options.text: A longer introduction at the start that sets the scene for the panel before they reach the recommendation
An assessment of the main risks and how they would be managed
More background on the department
A reference to the candidate's own experience

questions.hint: A recommendation should come with its risks and mitigations.

questions.prompt: Many case studies have no single right answer. How are they usually marked?

options.text: On how many facts from the pack you include
On the quality of your reasoning and communication
On whether you reach the preferred answer the panel has in mind, since case studies are written with a model solution
On the length of your answer

questions.hint: Marks follow criteria for analysis and judgement, not a hidden solution.

questions.prompt: If the case study is a discussion, what is a good habit?

options.text: Ask the panel what they think first
Wait until you are certain before you speak
Think aloud in a structured way and say what more you would want to know
Give your answer straight away and then defend it

questions.hint: Visible reasoning gives the panel evidence to score.

questions.prompt: The scenario involves delivery of a public service to vulnerable users. What should your recommendation consider?

options.text: The preferences of the most senior stakeholder
The cost alone, as the main constraint in public service delivery and the one most likely to be questioned afterwards
The effect on those users as well as cost and deadlines
The deadline alone, as the main constraint

questions.hint: Good decisions consider the people affected, not just internal factors.

questions.prompt: How should you finish a case-study discussion?

options.text: Repeat the main facts of the case
Summarise your recommendation, the reason for it and the first next step
Say that you would need more time to decide
Ask whether you have answered correctly

questions.hint: A clear closing summary shows you can land a message.

items.title: L11: In-tray exercises
items.body:
An in-tray exercise simulates a manager's inbox. You are given a set of emails, messages and documents, usually with a time limit, and asked to decide what to do with each: reply, delegate, escalate, schedule or ignore. It tests prioritisation, judgement, communication and sometimes the Civil Service Code. There may be an accompanying written task or a discussion in which you explain your choices.

The key skill is triage. Read everything quickly first, because a later item may change the priority of an earlier one: for example, a later email may show that two requests are in conflict, or that a task you plan to delegate is the responsibility of someone absent. Then sort items by urgency, which is about time, and importance, which is about consequences. Urgent and important items come first. Important but not urgent tasks need a scheduled time rather than being forgotten. Urgent but unimportant items may be delegated or answered briefly. Low-value items can wait or be declined.

Delegate sensibly: pass tasks to someone with the skills, capacity and authority, give clear instructions and a deadline, and follow up. Do not delegate something you are accountable for, such as a confidential matter, without safeguards. Escalate where the issue is beyond your authority, such as a potential security breach, a possible conflict of interest, or a request that seems improper.

In your replies, be brief and professional, note what you will do and by when, and explain your reasoning. Expect to find traps: a request from a senior person that conflicts with a rule, or confidential material copied to the wrong recipients. Spot them and act correctly.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of an in-tray exercise?

options.text: To measure how many emails you can answer in the time
To check you can memorise instructions
To test how quickly you can type and reply to messages, since a manager's day is mostly answering what arrives
To assess how you prioritise, make decisions and communicate under time pressure

questions.hint: It simulates the decisions a manager makes when work arrives from many directions.

questions.prompt: What is the sensible first step when you receive the in-tray papers?

options.text: Delegate everything straight away
Reply to the first email in full
Start with the longest document
Skim every item quickly to see how they relate before acting on any

questions.hint: Later items may change the priority or meaning of earlier ones.

questions.prompt: Which item should you deal with first?

options.text: An important task with a distant deadline
A request that is both urgent and important
A request that is urgent but of low importance, because the deadline is closer and others are waiting for it
A routine request from a friendly colleague

questions.hint: Urgent and important items have the greatest consequences and the shortest time.

questions.prompt: An important task has no immediate deadline. What is the best handling?

options.text: Schedule time for it so that it does not get forgotten
Delegate it without further instruction
Ask the sender to withdraw it for now
Leave it until the deadline gets closer, as there are more pressing demands and the task can be done quickly later

questions.hint: Important but not urgent work needs planned time.

questions.prompt: An email shows a colleague has sent confidential personal data to the wrong recipients. What should you do?

options.text: Delete your copy of the email and say nothing, because the mistake was made by someone else and is not yours to report
Follow the incident procedure, notify the right manager or data protection contact promptly and try to recall it
Wait to see whether anyone complains
Ask the recipients to ignore it and move on

questions.hint: A suspected data breach must be reported promptly under the proper procedure.

questions.prompt: When delegating an in-tray task, which action is most important?

options.text: Give clear instructions, a deadline and a way to check progress
Delegate without telling your manager
Delegate only the unimportant work
Tell the person to decide everything themselves

questions.hint: Clear delegation maintains accountability and quality.

questions.prompt: A senior colleague asks you to approve spending that would breach procurement rules. What is the best response?

options.text: Ignore the request and say nothing
Politely explain the rule, offer a compliant route and escalate if pressed
Approve it and mention it later
Approve it because of their seniority, on the basis that a senior colleague will have checked the rules already

questions.hint: The Civil Service Code requires integrity and proper handling of public money.

questions.prompt: Which reply to an email is most effective in an in-tray exercise?

options.text: A request for the sender to prioritise
A long explanation of your workload
A forward with no comment
A brief, professional message stating what you will do and by when

questions.hint: Replies should be clear, short and show your reasoning.

questions.prompt: Two requests from different senior people conflict. What should you do?

options.text: Do neither until one of them chases
Tell both, explain the conflict and ask them or a manager to agree priorities
Choose the more senior request and say nothing to the other person, since seniority is the usual tiebreak
Do part of each

questions.hint: Surfacing conflicts allows the right person to decide priorities.

questions.prompt: After the exercise, an interviewer asks why you postponed one task. What is the best response?

options.text: Say that you ran out of time
Explain the criteria you used, such as urgency, consequences and who else was affected
Say that you would now reverse the decision
Say that you did not think it mattered

questions.hint: Showing your criteria is what panels want to hear.

items.title: L11: Answering unexpected questions calmly
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Even well-prepared candidates meet an unexpected question: one that does not match any of your prepared examples, one about a gap in your experience, or a question you find uncomfortable. How you respond is itself evidence of composure, resilience and judgement.

The first technique is to pause. A few seconds of silence feels long to you and short to the panel. Use it to identify what the question is really testing: is it a Behaviour such as Working Together or Making Effective Decisions? Then choose the best-fitting example, even if it is not from your most recent job. Examples from voluntary work, studies or earlier roles are acceptable, if they provide evidence of the behaviour.

If you do not understand the question, ask for it to be repeated or rephrased. If you genuinely lack direct experience, say so briefly and then give the closest relevant evidence or describe how you would approach it. Do not invent. For a hypothetical or scenario question, show your reasoning step by step: what you would establish first, whom you would involve and what principles apply.

For uncomfortable questions, such as about a failure or a disagreement with a manager, answer factually without blaming others, and close with what you learned. If a question seems unfair or inappropriate, for example about your age, family plans or health, you can politely say that you would prefer to focus on the skills for the role, and raise it afterwards with the recruitment contact if it concerns you.

If you blank entirely, say you need a moment, or ask to return to the question later if the panel allows.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful first response to a question you did not prepare for?

options.text: Ask to skip the question
Answer at once with the nearest story you have, because a quick answer shows confidence and keeps the interview flowing
Say the question is unclear
Pause and work out which behaviour the question is really testing

questions.hint: Identifying the underlying behaviour helps you select suitable evidence.

questions.prompt: Which type of example is acceptable if you lack a recent workplace one?

options.text: Voluntary work, study or an earlier role, if it clearly evidences the behaviour
Only examples from within the Civil Service
None, as only your current job counts
Hypothetical examples about what you might do

questions.hint: Evidence matters more than where it comes from.

questions.prompt: The question has two parts and you remember only one. What is the best action?

options.text: Change the question into one you can answer
Ask the panellist to repeat the question
Give a general answer on the topic
Answer one part and hope it is enough, because asking for a repeat can look as though you were not listening

questions.hint: It is acceptable to ask for clarification.

questions.prompt: You have no direct experience of what the panel asks about. What is the best answer?

options.text: Invent an example to fill the gap, because a panel can only score evidence and a candidate with none will lose marks
Say so briefly and give the closest relevant evidence or your approach
Say that you will learn it on the job
Say the question is not relevant to the role

questions.hint: Honesty plus related evidence is credible and gives the panel something to score.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical question, what shows the strongest thinking?

options.text: Say that it depends and stop
Give a quick answer that sounds decisive
Explain step by step what you would establish, whom you would involve and which principles apply
Quote the relevant policy by number

questions.hint: Showing a method gives the panel reasoning to credit.

questions.prompt: Asked about a failure, how should you respond?

options.text: Choose a trivial failure and make light of it
Blame the circumstances
Describe it factually, take responsibility and explain what you learned
Say that you have never failed, since a panel wants to hear about success and not about mistakes at work

questions.hint: Learning from failure is a mark of resilience and self-awareness.

questions.prompt: The panel asks a question about your family plans. What is a suitable response?

options.text: Answer in full to avoid awkwardness, because refusing a question can look as though you have something to hide
Politely say you would prefer to focus on the skills for the role, and raise it afterwards if concerned
Leave the interview
Argue the point with the panel

questions.hint: Such questions are inappropriate and can be raised with the recruitment contact later.

questions.prompt: You blank completely. What should you do?

options.text: End the interview
Offer any example that comes to mind
Apologise repeatedly
Say you need a moment, breathe and then answer, or ask to return to it later

questions.hint: A short pause is acceptable and keeps you in control.

questions.prompt: Which statement about silence in interview is correct?

options.text: Silence always counts against the candidate, because the panel reads a pause as a sign that you lack knowledge
Silence indicates a lack of knowledge
A few seconds feels longer to you than to the panel and is acceptable
Silence is not allowed

questions.hint: Brief pauses show thoughtfulness.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to end an answer to an uncomfortable question about a disagreement with a manager?

options.text: Say you do not wish to discuss it
State what you learned and how you work with managers now
Say it was resolved
Describe the manager's faults

questions.hint: Ending with learning turns a difficult subject into evidence of growth.

items.title: L11: Using feedback after an interview
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance and Success Profiles (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Feedback is the most valuable thing to take from an unsuccessful promotion interview. Departments normally offer feedback if you ask, often by email or a short call from the panel chair or recruitment team. It is worth requesting promptly, while your memory of the interview is clear, and politely, saying you want to improve for next time.

Feedback usually refers to scores or descriptors against each Behaviour or strength, with comments such as 'gave limited evidence of own role' or 'did not cover the result'. Treat it as information about the evidence you gave, not a judgement of your worth. Listen without arguing: the purpose is not to change the outcome, which would be unusual. Ask clarifying questions: 'What would a stronger answer have included?' or 'Which part of the example lacked detail?' Write notes straight away.

Turn feedback into action. Identify the one or two patterns that cost you most marks, such as not describing the result or using 'we' too often. Write a short development plan: what you will change, how you will practise and by when. Practising aloud with a colleague or mentor helps, and so does rewriting your examples to fix the gaps. Also seek feedback from your manager on the Behaviours you are working on, and gather evidence between interviews through projects, stretch work or covering for a manager.

If you were successful, ask for feedback too, because it shows what to develop in the new role. Some departments hold reserve lists, so a strong performance can still lead to an offer later. Keep a record of your examples, updated as you gain new evidence.

questions.prompt: When is the best time to ask for interview feedback?

options.text: After six months, once you have had time to reflect and the panel has had time to forget the minor details
Only if you are successful
Only if you plan to appeal
Soon after the outcome, while the interview is fresh

questions.hint: Prompt requests help you and the panel remember specific detail.

questions.prompt: How should you respond when feedback seems harsh?

options.text: Dispute each point
Listen, note it and ask what a stronger answer would have included
End the conversation
Ask for a re-score

questions.hint: Using feedback as information helps you improve.

questions.prompt: Feedback says 'limited evidence of own role'. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Answers that were too short on background, because the panel did not have enough context to judge the example
Too many questions asked at the end
Poor eye contact
Overuse of 'we' and a lack of specific personal actions

questions.hint: Panels score personal contribution, which 'we' conceals.

questions.prompt: Feedback says you 'did not cover the result'. What is the best fix?

options.text: Add more background before the action, because a panel cannot judge the result without a full picture of the context
Shorten the action
Add a clear, specific outcome to each example, with measures where possible
Remove the example

questions.hint: The R in STAR provides proof of impact.

questions.prompt: What does an effective development plan after feedback look like?

options.text: A list of every area you could improve
A plan to apply to many roles at once
A plan to avoid interviews until you are ready
One or two specific changes, how you will practise them and by when

questions.hint: Focused, time-bound actions are more likely to be done.

questions.prompt: Why practise answers aloud?

options.text: It helps you remember scripts
Spoken answers are always shorter than written ones, so rehearsing aloud helps you fit them in the time allowed
Written answers can sound different when spoken, and speaking exposes gaps
It is required by the department

questions.hint: Rehearsal aloud tests clarity and timing.

questions.prompt: How can you gather new evidence between interviews?

options.text: Wait for the next vacancy to be advertised, and then think about how you would answer the likely questions
Repeat existing examples
Take on stretch work, lead a small project or cover for a manager
Ask for a promotion

questions.hint: New experiences produce fresh examples for future applications.

questions.prompt: Why ask for feedback if you were successful?

options.text: It lets you appeal
It lets you change your grade
It gives you a higher salary
It shows what to develop in the new role

questions.hint: Feedback helps you start well in the new role.

questions.prompt: What does a reserve list mean?

options.text: A list of candidates asked to retake
A list of internal candidates only
A list of candidates who passed but were not appointed, who may be offered a post later
A list of candidates who failed the interview and who may be invited to retry the process after a set waiting period

questions.hint: Strong candidates can still be offered posts if vacancies arise.

questions.prompt: Which action best prepares you for a future interview?

options.text: Avoid reviewing the old interview
Apply for the same role again immediately
Keep a record of examples and update them with new evidence and lessons
Memorise answers

questions.hint: A maintained bank of evidence makes preparation easier.
